⭐️ SEC eyes enforcement action over prediction market insider trading 

🔖 The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has warned that prediction markets offering contracts linked to corporate earnings and business performance could face enforcement action over insider trading, fraud and market manipulation. SEC Enforcement Director David Woodcock said the agency was monitoring activity on prediction platforms and expected to pursue potential securities violations. He added that enforcement activity was likely “in the future, for sure,” although he did not identify a particular company or announce new charges.

➡️ Woodcock’s comments centered on contracts that allow traders to bet on financial results or key performance indicators, commonly known as KPIs. Such products can involve outcomes tied to quarterly earnings, sales figures or other measures of a listed company’s business performance. The SEC oversees securities markets, while the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) regulates many derivatives contracts. Prediction markets can raise questions about which agency has authority when a contract’s outcome depends on a publicly traded company.

🔔 The regulator has already approved a Cboe Global Markets proposal involving binary options tied to corporate performance measures. The contracts allow traders to take positions on outcomes such as Citigroup’s earnings per share or Apple’s iPhone sales revenue. The decision addressed Cboe’s particular products and did not establish that every prediction contract involving a company’s performance automatically falls under SEC jurisdiction.

Crypto Idea

Alphabet was the first to plunge, losing about 13% and nearly $500 billion in market value following its earnings report, before continuing to slide the next day. Then Intel crashed by roughly 29%, even though its Data Center and AI division grew by 78%.

Taken together, these two stories look much more interesting than just two bad days for tech companies.

At Google, AI is growing at a breakneck pace, but the company has posted negative free cash flow for the second consecutive quarter. At Intel, demand for server solutions is enormous, but at the same time, the AI boom is draining memory supplies and manufacturing capacity away from the traditional PC market, which remains critical to the company. As a result, one of the biggest beneficiaries of AI is beginning to suffer from the consequences of the race itself.

And this raises a much more important question. Could this be the moment when the market finally stops focusing solely on AI growth rates and starts calculating how much this entire revolution actually costs?

Until now, the weak points of the AI race have mostly existed somewhere in the forecasts. 
Everyone understood that data centers cost enormous amounts of money, resources were in short supply, and returns on these investments would take time to materialize. Now, in just two days, the market has been given two very expensive demonstrations of these risks involving some of the world's largest tech companies.

And this could genuinely become dangerous for the entire market. That's because a significant portion of the S&P 500 and Nasdaq's growth over the past few years has been driven precisely by a handful of the largest tech companies and expectations surrounding AI. If the market starts reassessing how much Google, Microsoft, Amazon, Meta, Nvidia, and the rest should be worth in light of the actual cost of the AI race, we will be talking about much more than a correction in individual stocks.

At that point, the main question will no longer be which company is next. The real question will be how far the entire market could fall if the biggest driver of its growth in recent years suddenly becomes its biggest source of valuation risk.
